text: With a cataloged table in hand, it's finally time to run SQL. This lesson sets up Athena and runs the first real query against the files sitting in S3 — proving the pipeline actually works before tackling the stakeholder's real question.

There's one setup step first. Athena needs a query result location — a separate S3 path where it writes every query's output — and it simply won't run anything without one configured. That location is northfield-athena-results, deliberately separate from the raw zone, because writing results back into the raw data could get picked up by the next crawler run as if it were source data.

With that configured, the simplest useful query is select star from northfield underscore raw underscore db dot orders underscore raw, limit 10. That pulls ten real rows straight out of the CSV files in orders-raw, with no data warehouse and no loading step in between. If this returns real rows with the right columns, the entire chain from Lesson 1 through Lesson 5 just got proven out.
A second quick check is worth running too — a simple count of all rows in the table, which confirms all thirty-one days of August actually got picked up by the crawler, not just some of them.

It's worth understanding how this is actually billed. Athena charges by data scanned per query, roughly five dollars per terabyte, with a ten megabyte minimum per query. For a month of small CSV files — just a few megabytes total — this query costs a fraction of a cent. And if nobody runs a query, there's no bill at all. That's the real case for Athena over a warehouse at this scale.

This pricing model is also exactly why partitioning matters as data grows, which Lesson 8 comes back to. But first, next lesson writes the query that actually answers the Operations Manager's real question — units sold and revenue earned, by product category.
